title: How 2 Second-Year Backs Must REPLACE a Cleveland Browns Legend's 6,843-Yard Legacy
thumb_prompt: A worn, vintage Browns number 24 jersey draped over an empty locker stall in a dimly lit training facility, with two new jerseys numbered 10 and 22 hanging nearby in shadows, dramatic spotlight cutting through darkness
thumb_subject: a powerful running back in a brown and orange number 24 jersey, shown only as a fading silhouette

paragraphs.text: There is a ghost haunting the Browns running back room right now, and his name is Nick Chubb. Not the diminished version we saw hobbling through 2024 after two knee surgeries. Not the guy who signed with Houston last June. I am talking about the Nick Chubb who put up four straight thousand-yard seasons. The Chubb who finished with six thousand eight hundred forty-three rushing yards in seven years, third all-time in Browns history behind only Jim Brown and Leroy Kelly. The Chubb who averaged five point one yards per carry for his career. That ghost is everywhere at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus right now, and Quinshon Judkins and Dylan Sampson cannot escape it.

Let me tell you something about what the Browns lost when Chubb walked. They did not just lose a running back. They lost an identity. This was a guy who represented everything Cleveland wanted to be: tough, physical, relentless, humble. He set a franchise record with a ninety-two yard touchdown run as a rookie and never said a word about it afterward. Just a great job up front, he said. That was Nick Chubb. And now the Browns are asking two completely different second-year backs to somehow fill that void. It is not just about replacing production. It is about replacing what he meant.
card_lines: 51 career rushing TDs (3rd in Browns history)

paragraphs.text: The timing makes this even more fascinating. Chubb left Cleveland in June of twenty twenty-five, signing with the Texans after those brutal knee injuries derailed what should have been a Hall of Fame trajectory. The Browns had already drafted Judkins and Sampson in the twenty twenty-five draft, second and fourth rounds respectively. They knew Chubb was done. They knew they needed to rebuild the position. But here is what nobody talks about: they drafted two backs who could not be more different from each other, and neither one is remotely similar to the legend they are replacing. That tells you everything about where this franchise is heading.

Think about the Browns running back history for a second. Marion Motley. Jim Brown. Leroy Kelly. Those three are in the Hall of Fame. Chubb was on that path before the injuries hit. His yards per rush average of five point one is right there with Brown's five point two-one. He was just four hundred thirty-two yards shy of passing Leroy Kelly for second all-time in franchise rushing yards, and he did it in fifty-one fewer games. Fifty-one fewer games! The what-ifs will haunt Cleveland forever. What if he never gets hurt in Pittsburgh in twenty twenty-three? Could he have caught Jim Brown's twelve thousand three hundred twelve yards? We will never know.

sections.heading: Two Backs, Two Identities, One Massive Question

paragraphs.text: Now we get to the heart of the matter. Quinshon Judkins and Dylan Sampson are not just trying to replace Nick Chubb's production. They are trying to define what a Cleveland Browns running back looks like in the Todd Monken era, and so far nobody knows what that actually means. Judkins is the bruiser. Six feet, two hundred twenty-one pounds. Led the Browns with eight hundred twenty-seven rushing yards and seven touchdowns as a rookie in twenty twenty-five despite missing Week One and dealing with off-field issues that limited his training camp. But that three point six yards per carry? Dead last among qualified NFL backs. Forty-seventh in the entire league.
card_lines: Ended season: dislocated ankle, fractured fibula

paragraphs.text: Sampson is the complete opposite. Five-ten, smaller frame, SEC Offensive Player of the Year at Tennessee with fourteen hundred ninety-one yards and twenty-two touchdowns in his final college season. He came to Cleveland with elite receiving skills and home-run speed. But he got buried behind Judkins as a rookie, turning just sixty-five carries into one hundred seventy-five yards. That is two point seven yards per carry. Brutal. Yet when you watch the film, you see the talent. He caught thirty-three of forty targets for two hundred seventy-one yards and two touchdowns. He led all running backs in yards per route run at one point nine, tied with Bijan Robinson. The kid can play. He just never got the chance.
card_lines: 1.90 yards per route run (1st among RBs)

paragraphs.text: Here is where it gets really interesting. Todd Monken comes from Baltimore, where he just watched Derrick Henry and Justice Hill dominate with a thunder-and-lightning approach. Monken himself compared Judkins and Sampson to that dynamic. Baltimore ranked first in rushing yards per game in twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-four, and second in twenty twenty-five under Monken's offense. The blueprint is right there. But here is the problem: Derrick Henry was getting twenty-plus carries every single week and actually producing with them. Judkins got that volume as a rookie and could not crack four yards per carry. That is a massive red flag.

The Browns are banking everything on Judkins bouncing back from that ankle injury and fractured fibula he suffered in Week Sixteen. He was at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus throughout the entire offseason program, grinding through rehab. Monken has been raving about him in training camp, calling him fun to watch. But you know what? Coaches always say that stuff in August. The real question is whether the offensive line can give him anything to work with. You remember what we saw in twenty twenty-five. That line was a disaster. If Andrew Berry truly fixed it like he claims, then maybe Judkins can be the workhorse. If not, we are looking at another year of two point yard carries and wasted potential.

And what about Sampson? The dude has been nicked up at training camp according to Monken. That is concerning. But when he is healthy, the potential is undeniable. Monken wants to use him as a true satellite back, getting him into space on passing downs, letting him work out of the slot, creating mismatches against linebackers. That SEC Offensive Player of the Year season at Tennessee was not a fluke. The guy had over fourteen hundred rushing yards and scored twenty-two times on the ground. He can do everything. The Browns just have to actually use him. If Sampson can stay healthy and carve out a consistent role, this backfield suddenly has a real identity.
card_lines: Mismatches vs linebackers in passing game

sections.heading: What This Tells Us About Cleveland's Identity Crisis

paragraphs.text: Let us zoom out for a second and talk about what this running back situation reveals about the Browns as a whole. For years, Cleveland built its identity around Nick Chubb and a smash-mouth running game. It was simple. It was physical. It worked when the line blocked. Now they have two young backs with completely different skill sets, a first-time head coach in Monken trying to install a complex scheme, and an offensive line that might have five new starters. Do you see the problem? The Browns do not know who they are anymore. They are stuck between what they used to be and what they are trying to become.
card_lines: Old identity: Chubb + power run game

paragraphs.text: The Monken hire tells you everything. This is not Kevin Stefanski's run-heavy, play-action offense anymore. Monken wants to push tempo, use pre-snap motion and shifts to attack the second level of defenses, create explosive plays in the passing game. That sounds great on paper. But you need the horses to run it. You need an offensive line that can handle complex assignments and pick up blitzes. You need running backs who can pass protect, catch out of the backfield, and still pound the rock when you need four yards. Do Judkins and Sampson fit that profile? We are about to find out.

Here is my take. I think Sampson is the more natural fit for what Monken wants to do. His receiving ability and speed in space are elite. He can line up anywhere and create problems. But Judkins has the size and mentality to be a true number one back if he can just get back to what he showed at Ohio State. The problem is neither guy has proven they can carry a full NFL workload yet. Judkins broke down with injuries. Sampson barely got on the field. And now the Browns are asking them to replace a legend who gave them seven years of elite, durable production. The odds are not in their favor.

This Saturday's preseason game against the Bears is going to be fascinating. We will finally see Judkins and Sampson running behind whatever version of this offensive line takes the field. We will see if Monken's scheme actually translates from Baltimore to Cleveland. We will see if these two young backs have taken the necessary steps forward. But more than anything, we will see whether the Browns have truly moved on from the Nick Chubb era or if they are still desperately trying to recreate something that is gone forever. My gut says it is the latter. Ghosts are hard to shake.

Can they move past Chubb's legacy?

sections.heading: The Bigger Picture Nobody Wants to Admit

paragraphs.text: Let me hit you with some hard truth. The Browns have not had a home playoff game at Huntington Bank Field in its entire twenty-five year history. Think about that for a second. Twenty-five years. Zero home playoff games. The stadium is moving to Brook Park in about four years, and if they do not get at least one playoff game in that building before it closes, it will be one of the most embarrassing statistics in Browns history. And you know what the foundation of playoff football is? Running the damn ball. Controlling the clock. Winning in the trenches. All the things Nick Chubb represented.
card_lines: 0 home playoff games at Huntington Bank
Moving to Brook Park in ~4 years
Playoff success built on run game

paragraphs.text: That is why this running back situation matters so much. It is not just about Judkins and Sampson putting up fantasy points or hitting certain yardage totals. It is about whether this team can establish a physical identity that wins games in December and January. Cleveland plays in the AFC North. You have to run the football to survive in this division. Baltimore does it with Henry. Pittsburgh has always done it with whoever is back there. The Bengals might be pass-heavy but they have Joe Burrow. What do the Browns have? A quarterback competition that still is not settled and two unproven running backs trying to fill shoes they will never actually fill.

I keep going back to what Chubb meant to this franchise beyond the stats. He was the one constant during years of chaos. Quarterback carousel? Chubb was there, grinding out tough yards. Coaching changes? Chubb was there, producing. Front office turnover? Chubb was there, being the ultimate professional. When Jim Brown died in June of twenty twenty-three, Chubb talked about carrying on the legacy of Brown and Herschel Walker, the two greats he grew up idolizing. He took that responsibility seriously. Now the Browns need Judkins or Sampson to do the same thing, and I am just not sure either one of them understands the weight of that yet.
card_lines: Vowed to honor Jim Brown's legacy

paragraphs.text: The unofficial depth chart that dropped on Monday has Judkins listed as the starter with Sampson behind him and Raheim Sanders in the three-hole. That rotation makes sense on paper. But depth charts in August mean absolutely nothing. What matters is who can stay healthy, who can produce when the games matter, and who can help this offense find an identity. If Judkins can get back to his Ohio State form and Sampson can carve out that satellite role, maybe this works. Maybe the Browns actually evolve into something new and dangerous. Or maybe they spend all season chasing the ghost of number twenty-four and never figure out who they really are.

One more thing. The Browns running back room has a unique challenge that nobody else in the league faces. They are not just replacing a good player. They are replacing a franchise icon who finished third all-time in rushing yards behind two Hall of Famers, who made four straight Pro Bowls, who embodied everything Cleveland football is supposed to be. Marion Motley averaged five point seven yards per carry. Jim Brown averaged five point two-one. Nick Chubb averaged five point one before the injuries destroyed his final two seasons. That is the company we are talking about. Judkins and Sampson are not walking into a normal situation. They are walking into history, and history has very high expectations.
card_lines: Browns RB tradition: Motley, Brown, Kelly

paragraphs.text: So here is what I am watching this preseason and into the regular season. Can Judkins prove that three point six yards per carry was an anomaly caused by a bad offensive line and not a reflection of who he actually is? Can Sampson stay healthy and force Monken to get him the ball in creative ways? Can these two backs develop any kind of chemistry and complementary rhythm? And most importantly, can the Browns finally accept that Nick Chubb is gone and build something new instead of constantly looking backward? The answers to those questions will define Cleveland's entire season. And maybe, just maybe, determine whether this franchise can finally break through and give the fans something to believe in again.
card_lines: Can Browns move past Chubb era?

sections.heading: The Verdict on Cleveland's Running Back Gamble

paragraphs.text: Look, I am not saying Judkins and Sampson are going to fail. I am saying they are in an impossible situation. Replacing Nick Chubb is hard enough. Doing it while the entire offense is being overhauled under a new head coach, with a rebuilt offensive line, and an unsettled quarterback situation makes it damn near impossible. But that is the hand they have been dealt. The Browns did not have a choice. Chubb's body broke down. He signed with Houston. The page turned whether Cleveland was ready or not. Now Judkins and Sampson have to write the next chapter, and it better be a good one.
card_lines: Add: new coach, new O-line, QB battle

paragraphs.text: The good news? Todd Monken knows how to build a running game. He did it in Baltimore with inferior talent compared to what Derrick Henry brought. He did it in Georgia when he was the offensive coordinator there. The man understands how to create explosive runs through scheme, and if anyone can maximize Judkins' power and Sampson's versatility, it is him. The bad news? This is the NFL, and scheme only gets you so far. You need players who can execute, who can stay healthy, who can perform when the moment is big. We do not know if Judkins and Sampson can do that yet. We are all just hoping.
card_lines: Built elite rushing attacks in Baltimore

paragraphs.text: The Browns are betting their entire offensive identity on two second-year backs who combined for barely over a thousand yards as rookies and looked shaky doing it. That is a massive gamble. But sometimes gambles pay off. Sometimes you draft two running backs in the same draft and they become the next great one-two punch. Sometimes the pieces just fit. I want to believe that is what happens here. I want to believe Judkins becomes the bruising between-the-tackles runner who grinds out tough yards and moves the chains. I want to believe Sampson becomes the home-run threat who breaks games open with his speed and receiving ability. I want to believe the Browns find their identity and finally become a playoff team again.

But belief does not win football games. Execution does. And right now, the Cleveland Browns have more questions than answers at the most important position on their offense. Can they replace Nick Chubb's six thousand eight hundred forty-three yards with two unproven backs who are nothing like him? Can they build an identity that works in the brutal AFC North? Can they finally give the fans something to cheer about after decades of disappointment? The answers start this Saturday in Chicago. The ghosts of Browns running backs past will be watching. So will we. Let us see if Quinshon Judkins and Dylan Sampson are ready to carry the weight of all that history on their shoulders. Because ready or not, that is exactly what Cleveland is asking them to do.
card_lines: Ready or not, it's their time
